build_vs_buy.criticality_why: VERDICT: important. Changed from "critical".
build_vs_buy.best_icp: Sell first to small and mid-size US local governments (about 10k to 150k residents) running permitting and business licensing on aging systems such as Naviline/CentralSquare on AS/400 (Branson, MO is one), low-end tools or spreadsheets: they pay about $50k to $300k a year, buy rather than build, and approve contracts at a single council meeting (La Palma, South Charleston, Shelbyville), whereas the largest cities and states need $15M+ citywide or multi-year programmes, often build or heavily customise (NYC DOB NOW, California BreEZe, New Hampshire on Salesforce), and buy slowly under heavy scrutiny (San Francisco's OpenGov award drew a Budget and Legislative Analyst review).

enterprise.evidence:
NOT A BUYER. Spend is null. Unchanged from the original.

Why: issuing permits and licences is a government function. Large private companies are applicants, not issuers.
- What they buy instead is applicant-side tooling. Example: PermitFlow, whose clients include Lennar and Amazon. That is a separate category (from the earlier research; not re-checked here).
- Industrial 'permit-to-work' systems (oil and gas, utilities) share the name. They are safety (EHS) software, not licensing case management.
- The closest private match is self-regulatory bodies that license their members, such as FINRA. They are few, quasi-public, and mostly build their own systems. Too thin to size.

No filing or tender was found showing a private enterprise buying Accela, EnerGov, Idox or similar for its own use.

name: Government tax administration
systems: IRS Individual Master File (IMF) and Business Master File (BMF): IBM-built 1960s mainframe, COBOL and Assembly (US)
IRS CADE 2 (replacement program for IMF, in build since 2010)
FAST Enterprises GenTax (COTS integrated tax system, 60+ agencies, US states and abroad)
SAP ECC 6.0 based tax platforms, e.g. HMRC Enterprise Tax Management Platform (ETMP), 45+ tax regimes (UK)
ATO National Taxpayer System (NTS, 1975) and ATO Integrated System (AIS, 1994), partly replaced by Accenture-built Integrated Core Processing (ICP) (AU)
DJP SIDJP (Indonesia core tax system in use since 2002), replaced by Coretax (LG CNS-Qualysoft)
India Income Tax e-filing and Centralised Processing Centre (CPC 1.0, then CPC 2.0 by Infosys)
Vietnam GDT TMS centralized tax management application (rolled out 2014-2015, replaced 16 distributed apps)
Singapore IRAS IRIN (Inland Revenue Interactive Network) integrated system
In-house mainframe systems at state revenue departments and local property/council tax billing systems
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Tax administration is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software at the national level in the US, UK and AU. Each agency is a single sovereign buyer that cannot interrupt revenue collection, and it carries decades of annually amended tax law encoded in COBOL. It is less locked in SEA, where Vietnam, Indonesia and India replaced their cores between 2014 and 2025.

s1.why: Primary government sources cover the largest installed cores in several in-scope countries. GAO-25-107795 lists two Treasury tax processing systems aged 59 and 51 years, both on COBOL and Assembly. CRS IF12525 dates the IRS IMF to the 1960s. IGT/ANAO date ATO NTS to 1975 and AIS to 1994. The NAO (via The Register) reports 124 HMRC legacy systems still running in March 2024, some over 30 years old. The common replacements are also pre-cloud and on-prem in origin: FAST GenTax was built as late-1990s client-server and SAP ECC 6.0 is from 2006. Caveat: the SEA cores are newer (Vietnam TMS 2014-15, Indonesia Coretax 2025, India CPC 2.0 from 2019), so the sign holds at US/UK/AU national level and much less in VN/ID/IN.

s2.why: Several jurisdictions have primary, quantified timelines. IRS CADE 2 started in 2010 and targets FY2028, after CADE 1 was abandoned in 2009, and IMF replacement projects were suspended in May 2024 (CRS). The ATO Change Program ran Dec 2003 to June 2010, cost A$756.7m and left BAS and SG undelivered (IGT). HMRC's SAP S/4HANA contract runs to 2035. Indonesia's Coretax took from 2018 to a Dec 2024 build and a 2026 handover. The India CPC 2.0 8.5-year term comes only from search snippets and does not count.

s3.why: The only quantified evidence is from one agency. The National Taxpayer Advocate says IRS staff key in paper returns digit by digit, with transcription errors on about 22% of them and a backlog near 15M returns in 2022. That is mainly a paper-intake gap, not a spreadsheet or screen-scraping workaround for core-system limits. The ATO data synchronisation claim comes from a search summary and was not opened. Nothing was found for HMRC, the EU, or the SEA agencies.

s4.why: GAO says the two Treasury tax systems run on COBOL and Assembly, which have a dwindling pool of skilled people. The line about paying a premium for contractors is GAO's general statement across agencies, not one specific to tax. The $754m a year in the earlier research is wrong: it covers all 11 federal legacy systems. There is no quantified evidence of a skills shortage for the dominant non-US platforms (GenTax, SAP ECC, ICP, TMS, Coretax), and SAP/GenTax skills are not notably scarce. This rests on one agency's evidence.

reasons_to_stay: Failed or troubled replacements make agencies cautious: IRS CADE 1 was abandoned in 2009 after cost overruns, the ATO's 2010 ICP rollout caused processing problems and left BAS and SG on legacy, and Indonesia's Coretax drew taxpayer complaints at its 2025 launch.
Revenue continuity: the systems collect a large share of government revenue (HMRC ETMP handles about GBP 800bn a year), so cutover risk is political.
Tax law changes every year, and decades of encoded rules in COBOL/Assembly are hard to extract and re-validate.
Funding is lumpy and political: IRS IRA modernization money may run out by FY2026 and IMF replacement projects were suspended in 2024.
Procurement and sovereignty constraints: long tenders, single-source awards (SAP's GBP 275m HMRC award), and sovereign-cloud and security accreditation needs.
Incumbent integrator and COTS lock-in: Aspire-era contracts, GenTax configuration, and maintenance contracts after go-live (LG CNS kept maintenance after the Coretax handover).

SUMMARY
- Government is the only segment that buys this system.
- Typical annual spend runs from about $5k for a small town to about $150m for a large national agency. The IRS is left out as an outlier.
- Spend depends mostly on the level of government, so the range is built up from four tiers below.

HOW TO READ THIS
- Annual figure = contract value divided by its term. Where a figure includes implementation, that is stated.
- Staff costs are excluded where the source separates them.
- Tags: [verified] means the source was opened and the figure matched. [search only] means the figure came from a search summary because the page returned 403. [corrected] means this review changed the number.
- FX assumptions: GBP 1 = about $1.30, EUR 1 = about $1.10, INR 70 = $1 (2019 rate), IDR 14,500 = $1 (2020 rate).

CHANGES MADE IN THIS REVIEW
1. Low end of the range cut from $10k to $5k. The original tier 1 cited $1k-10k figures but set the floor at $10k, which did not match. The new floor is still within 2x of the old one.
2. Newcastle-under-Lyme raised from GBP 71k to GBP 235k a year. The current NEC contract (from May 2023, hosted) is GBP 235k a year, GBP 2.27m over up to 7 years. The old GBP 71k could not be traced and is more than 3x too low for today's spend.
3. Tandridge raised from GBP 70k to about GBP 95k a year: GBP 70k licence plus GBP 25k support.
4. India's 8.5-year term is now confirmed (Cabinet approval, Jan 2019). The outlay includes GST, rent, postage and project managem

name: Insurance claims management
systems: In-house mainframe / midrange claims systems (COBOL, IBM z/OS, IBM i / AS400 RPG) at carriers, many 20+ years old
Guidewire ClaimCenter (on-prem Java versions, first sold 2003; now moving to Guidewire Cloud)
DXC Assure Claims, formerly CSC / DXC RISKMASTER (corporate risk, self-insured, TPA claims)
FINEOS Claims / AdminSuite (life, accident, health, group and absence claims; company founded 1993)
Duck Creek Claims
Sapiens claims products (IDIT, ClaimsPro / ClaimsMaster)
Majesco P&C Core Suite Claims
Insurity claims (Sure Suite)
Fadata INSIS (EMEA composite core incl. claims)
Lloyd's / London market bureau claims infrastructure (ECF, with re-keying into managing-agent systems)
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Claims is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. Systems hold open reserves, litigation files and regulator-mandated history that must be migrated intact, and they connect to policy, payments, reinsurance and fraud tools. Unlike policy admin, though, claims is often the first core module carriers replace, and AI overlays (fraud, triage, damage estimation) can sit on top of the incumbent without replacing it.

s1.why: Primary sources date the dominant installed claims systems to before 2005, all on-prem. Guidewire's 2011 S-1 says P&C carriers run core systems often 20+ years old on outdated languages. Guidewire first sold ClaimCenter, now the most widely installed packaged claims system (270+ customers), in 2003 as on-prem Java software. RISKMASTER dates from the early 1980s and FINEOS was founded in 1993. Datos Insights (Apr 2025) quantifies it: over 50% of insurers still manage claims on legacy platforms. Two caveats. The Datos figure covers life, annuity and benefits only. The S-1 is a vendor describing the systems it wants to replace.

s2.why: Two vendors say this in their own SEC filings. Guidewire's FY2025 10-K puts initial subscription terms at usually five years, with some of seven years or longer, and calls sales cycles lengthy. Its S-1 says implementation runs 6 to 24+ months. Sapiens' FY2024 20-F says sales cycles run 1 to 2 years and delivery takes from several months to a few years. Taken together, a carrier commits to the system for several years from evaluation to go-live and beyond. The strict 7+ year contract term applies only to some Guidewire deals, so the grade rests on multi-year replacement rather than on contract length.

s3.why: The only primary source is Lloyd's Blueprint Two, which documents re-keying, manual extraction and spreadsheet bordereaux. It covers London market delegated-authority and bureau claims data, not the carrier claims systems that dominate the category. The 72% Excel/homegrown statistic comes from an industry report with no named author, relayed by ClaimsPages. No quantified source shows screen-scraping or re-keying around ClaimCenter or mainframe claims cores across carriers in general.

s4.why: Guidewire's 2011 S-1 says retiring staff are hard to replace. That is a vendor claim from 15 years ago about the systems it sells against. The Rocket Software survey (52% struggle to find legacy-skilled staff, 35% say they have adequate skills) covered 276 IT leaders across industries. It is not insurance-specific, and the article only adds insurance context in commentary. No claims-specific or insurer-specific quantified skills data exists. For ClaimCenter/Gosu, the dominant installed system, the evidence points to a large Guidewire SI talent pool, mostly in India, more than to scarcity.

reasons_to_stay: Long contracts: Guidewire initial terms run five years with annual renewals, and some run seven years or longer, which locks in the incumbent.
Implementation risk and time: 6 to 24+ months per Guidewire's S-1 and 'several months to a few years' per Sapiens. Claims history must be migrated (for example, Heritage converted about 240k claims).
Claims systems link to policy admin, payments, reserving, reinsurance, fraud tools and regulator reporting, so a swap touches many integrations.
Regulatory and audit continuity: claims reserves, litigation files and regulator-mandated data (for example, Lloyd's ECF and bureau messaging) must stay intact.
Sunk configuration: decades of customer-specific business rules live in the incumbent system.
Vendors offer an upgrade path instead of replacement (Guidewire Cloud, DXC AWS hosting), so carriers modernise in place.
High retention signals inertia (DXC cites 98.5%+ customer retention).

build_vs_buy.criticality_why: Verdict: critical for insurers. Important (not critical) for self-insured buyers. The original call holds.
build_vs_buy.best_icp: Start with lower mid-market carriers, MGAs and TPAs, roughly $50M to $1B in premium: they rarely build in-house, many still run 20-year-old cores that their retiring staff can no longer maintain, they decide faster than enterprise carriers locked into five-year Guidewire terms, and they spend about $250K to $1.5M a year on claims, which is enough to fund an AI-native claims core; once there are references, add self-insured counties and risk pools ($40K to $250K a year, fast SaaS buys), then bid on state-fund replacements such as NYSIF's open claims RFP.

mid_market.evidence:
WHO: regional carriers and mutuals, state funds run like carriers, and larger third-party administrators (TPAs). Roughly $100M to $1B in DWP.

BUILD VS BUY: some.
- Many still run claims cores built in-house decades ago. Guidewire's 2011 S-1 (verified) says carriers' legacy cores have 'often been in operation for 20 years or more' and that the IT staff who maintain them 'are retiring and hard to replace'.
- When these buyers replace a system today, they almost always buy a package rather than build a new one. Their IT teams are too small for a new build.

SPEND: about $250K to $1.5M a year on claims. Steps:
(1) Majesco, which sells mostly to mid-size P&C carriers (verified): FY25 revenue over $300M. It reports 375+ customers after the Vitech deal, of which 275+ are P&C. Before Vitech the base was about 300 customers, so about $1M per customer per year for the full suite including services. 95% of customers are on Majesco's cloud.
(2) Duck Creek FY2022 10-K (verified): $302.9M revenue across 150+ customers, about $2M each for all products. Its base skews larger, since it serves four of the top five North American carriers.
(3) Software price-comparison sites cite Duck Creek Claims and Sapiens ClaimsPro quotes starting around $100K+ a year. (Search snippet only. Weak evidence.)
(4) Claims is about 25% to 40% of suite spend. That gives about $250K to $800K a year in subscription and support. Implementation services in the replacement years push the top toward $1.5M.

RESULT: abo

smb.evidence:
WHO: small carriers under about $100M DWP, managing general agents (MGAs), small TPAs and self-insured employers. Ordinary small businesses that are not insurers do not buy claims systems.

BUILD VS BUY: rare. These buyers have no development team. They run vendor-hosted packages or spreadsheets. Lloyd's Blueprint Two describes re-keying and manual claims handling among coverholders and managing agents in the delegated-authority market.

SPEND: about $25K to $250K a year. Steps:
(1) Per-seat SaaS: software price-comparison sites cite about $50 to $150 per user per month for standalone claims platforms. For 10 to 50 adjusters that is about $6K to $90K a year. (Secondary source. Weak evidence.)
(2) Real contracts for similar-size buyers, both with Origami Risk, which Guidewire's 10-K names as a competitor (both verified from the contract PDFs):
  - Charlotte County, FL: RMIS claims management at $43,000 a year, $129,000 over 3 years (Oct 2021 to Sept 2024).
  - Marion County, OR: 5-year contract worth $695,625. Year one is $221,025 (subscription plus one-time fees), then $118,650 a year.
(3) Five Sigma (verified): it prices with a scoped launch package, an annual platform fee and usage fees. Its Starter tier is aimed at teams modernizing for the first time. No dollar amounts are published.
(4) Small regulated carriers sit at the top of the range. They need full reserving, payments and regulatory reporting, not just claim tracking.

RESULT: about $25K to $250K a year. No change

government.evidence:
Government buyers fall into two very different groups. That is why the range is wide.

GROUP 1: counties, cities and risk pools that insure themselves. They buy SaaS RMIS or claims systems. Typical spend is $40K to $250K a year.

DXC Assure Integral and Assure Ingenium (multiline/life PAS)

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: More legacy-locked than a typical enterprise category because life and annuity policies stay in force for decades. Insurers have to keep servicing closed books on the original mainframe or AS/400 PAS, and many run several PAS at once. P&C is the exception: Tier-1 carriers there have largely moved to post-2005 cores such as Guidewire and Duck Creek.

s1.why: Deloitte's Dec 2022 survey of 100 L&A CIOs found two-thirds run more than one PAS and 23% run more than four. 43% say they will not retire any legacy core system once modernization is done (77% in the smallest revenue band). Deloitte also says many life insurers still run mainframe-based legacy cores. Product histories support this: DXC PMS/Series II dates from the 1970s on z/OS, CyberLife from 1995 on z/OS, and the SMART400/LifeAsia/POLISY family runs on AS/400 (Celent says it is still in use). Caveat: the quantified evidence covers life and annuity. In US/UK Tier-1 P&C, Guidewire PolicyCenter (2006) and Duck Creek have replaced much of the pre-2005 base, so the sign is weaker for P&C. The 68% 'legacy PAS' figure in search results comes from a market-research mill and should not be cited.

s2.why: Primary filings from the main replacement vendors show this directly. Guidewire's FY2025 10-K says initial subscription terms are generally five years, some seven years or longer, with extensive evaluation cycles. Majesco's 2019 10-K cites multi-year agreements of 5-7 years. Sapiens' 2024 20-F gives a 1-2 year sales cycle and delivery of months to years. Deloitte's L&A survey describes a 'multiyear time horizon' to implement. One DXC conversion of 17 source systems took 3 years (a single case study).

s3.why: The only cited evidence is vendor marketing from Pace, an AI-agent startup. It says its agents drive green-screen and legacy admin systems, and claims about 90% task resolution at one customer (Palomar). That is one vendor and anecdotal. The McKinsey rekeying figure was never opened, and Accenture-style underwriter-time figures cover underwriting, not policy admin. Re-keying across multiple PAS is plausible given that two-thirds of L&A carriers run more than one PAS (Deloitte), but no source quantifies spreadsheet use, re-keying or screen-scraping against policy admin systems.

s4.why: The Rocket Software survey (n=276: 52% find legacy skills hard to hire, 35% say they have adequate skills) covers IT leaders at large enterprises in all industries, not insurers. Deloitte's L&A piece says only that legacy mainframe staff 'may be retired or retiring'. Celent makes the same point qualitatively. The LifeAsia/AS400 evidence is training-vendor copy and a few Kuala Lumpur job ads. No quantified, insurance-specific source shows a shortage of PAS skills.

reasons_to_stay: Reliability and stability for mission-critical processing. Celent cites this as why SMART400/Polisy/400/Life/400 remain in use.
The need to keep ongoing business running during change (Celent).
Replacement cost and risk: sales cycles of 1-2 years and delivery of months to years (Sapiens 20-F). Subscriptions run 5-7+ years (Guidewire 10-K, Majesco 10-K).
Data conversion complexity: one DXC migration moved 719,000 policy records from 17 source systems, some up to 40 years old, over 3 years.
Long-tail closed books: life and annuity policies stay in force for decades, so old products must keep being serviced.
Tightly coupled surrounding applications. A MassMutual executive cited apps tightly coupled to DXC platforms as an enabler for rehosting rather than replacing.

Regulatory reporting and actuarial logic embedded in legacy code, with outsourced AMS contracts. DXC has run application outsourcing for a VANTAGE-ONE annuity block for about 20 years (search snippet).

build_vs_buy.criticality_why: VERDICT: critical. Confirmed on review, with one weak argument replaced.
build_vs_buy.best_icp: Sell first to mid-market carriers and large MGAs with about $100M-1B DWP. Why this tier: (1) Each spends $0.5M-3M a year on the system, enough to support a real contract. (2) Many still run ageing AS/400 or COBOL cores, and the staff who know them are retiring. (3) They almost never build in-house, so they will buy. (4) Each deal is far smaller than a Tier 1 programme, which lowers the buyer's risk. The 1-2 year sales cycle Sapiens reports is an all-tier figure, so do not assume mid-market deals close much faster. Two ways in avoid a risky full core replacement on day one: an AI layer over the legacy core, or one new product line or closed block on a new system. Small mutuals and new MGAs are a faster but smaller second target: published SaaS prices start at about $12K a year, and Novarica reports more small insurers now looking to replace.

systems: Sunquest Laboratory (Clinisys, formerly Roper; InterSystems Cache/MUMPS database, AIX/OpenVMS/Linux/Windows)

Epic Beaker (Chronicles/InterSystems-based, bundled with Epic EHR)
Clinisys WinPath / WinPath Enterprise (UK NHS)
Telepath (CSC/iSOFT/DXC, now managed by Dedalus in the NHS)
iLab APEX (UK NHS)
Orchard Harvest LIS (now Clinisys)
Auslab (PJA Solutions / Citadel Health, Queensland Health)
TECHNIDATA TDNexLabs
Evident (CPSI) Thrive EHR-LIS
Meditech LIS
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: LIS is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. Every change has to be revalidated under CLIA, CAP or ISO 15189, blood-bank modules are FDA-regulated devices, and decades of analyzer interfaces build up. In US hospitals, though, the systems are being replaced faster than in most legacy categories, because LIS moves with the EHR into Epic Beaker.

s1.why: In the CAP TODAY Nov 2020 LIS guide, several vendors report their own first installation dates. Together they cover most of the installed base. TECHNIDATA 1973, Sunquest 1979 (the Clinisys history page says the first lab install was 1981), Cerner PathNet 1982, SCC SoftLab 1985, Evident 1986, Orchard Harvest 1993. These run on InterSystems Cache/MUMPS or on Oracle over AIX, HP-UX or VMS, all on-prem client-server or midrange. UK WinPath (1992) and Telepath (1980s/1990s) and Australia's Auslab (c.1996) fit the same pattern. One caveat: Epic Beaker is the fastest-growing US hospital LIS and is a newer module (late 2000s). It does sit on Epic's pre-2005 Chronicles/Cache core, so the sign holds across the category.

s2.why: The UK competition regulator states it directly in its Roper/CliniSys decision (para 50): NHS LIMS contracts 'typically run for between five and ten years, often with options for extension'. That is a regulator finding for a whole national market, not one vendor. Queensland Health is a concrete case of a multi-year replacement. It awarded a 10-year, $64m Sunquest project in Feb 2018 to replace Auslab. It spent $37.5m, cancelled in 2020 after quality delays, and extended support for the 1990s-era Auslab from 2020 to 2029 (itnews). One limit: 5 to 10 years only partly meets the 7+ year threshold. The 13-year Kent and Medway figure rests on unopened search snippets.

s3.why: Re-keying is documented, but the evidence is narrow and anecdotal. JAMIA (2019) found a 3.7% transcription error rate when staff re-keyed point-of-care glucose results into the EHR. That study covered 60 clinics at two centres, and the gap sits at the device and EHR boundary, not inside the core LIS. In CAP TODAY (Nov 2022), Henry Ford's lab IT head says molecular results are still typed into the LIS by hand. No cross-lab survey quantifies spreadsheet or re-keying workarounds around the dominant LIS products.

s4.why: This is plausible but not shown for these systems specifically. Sunquest and Epic run on InterSystems Cache/MUMPS, and SCC and Cerner run on AIX/VMS/HP-UX, which are niche stacks. The only staffing evidence is general. In CAP TODAY (Nov 2022), vendors say one large institution has 110+ critical IT vacancies and that lab personnel shortages limit LIS implementation. The widely cited 20-25k shortfall is for bench technologists, not LIS analysts. No primary source (GAO, a workforce survey, or job-market data) shows that Sunquest, SoftLab, PathNet or WinPath skills are scarce. The GAO pages checked earlier mention COBOL, not MUMPS.

reasons_to_stay: Regulated validation: every LIS change must be revalidated under CLIA/CAP/ISO 15189, so switching costs are high
Deep instrument and middleware interfaces (analyzers, blood bank, microbiology) built up over decades
Tight coupling to the EHR: Epic Beaker and Cerner PathNet come bundled with the hospital EHR contract
Failed replacements: Queensland Health spent $37.5m on a Sunquest replacement, cancelled it, and kept Auslab to 2029
Long contracts: NHS LIMS contracts run 5-10 years with extensions, and network-wide programmes run up to 13 years
Decades of historical results must be migrated (Auslab held 17 years and 4 billion+ result sets per search snippet)
Blood bank modules are FDA-regulated medical devices (e.g. Sunquest device recalls), which raises the replacement bar

name: Land and property registry
systems: US county recorder land-records systems: Tyler Technologies Eagle Recorder / EagleSoftware, Harris Recording Solutions OnCore (legacy, 2003) and Acclaim, Fidlar AVID/Laredo, Kofile, Catalis Official Records, Infocon County systems on IBM AS/400 (IBM i)
HM Land Registry (England and Wales) core register on a mainframe (140M documents, about 1 PB), plus the eDRS scanned-form channel, now retired
Queensland Automated Titles System (ATS, from 1994)
Landgate WA Smart Register (replaced 2015 to 2017 by NLR-T/Advara)
NSW LRS and Victoria SERV registries (privatised under 35- and 40-year concessions)
Singapore SLA INLIS (1998) and the Land Titles registry
India: Bhoomi (Karnataka, NIC, 1999-2001), state RoR systems under DILRMP, NGDRS e-registration
Indonesia ATR/BPN KKP (Komputerisasi Kegiatan Pertanahan): desktop, then Geo-KKP, then KKP-Web
Malaysia SPTB (Sistem Pendaftaran Tanah Berkomputer, 1995) and e-Tanah
Philippines LRA Land Titling Computerization Project (LARES, BOO, awarded 2000)
Vietnam district- and province-level land databases (VILG/MPLIS) moving to a national land database
Thailand Department of Lands Land Information System
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: The register carries a state guarantee of title and is bound to local land law. That makes it more locked in than typical enterprise software: replacements need statutory change, decades-long concessions and bulk data migration. But the cores are mostly bespoke systems from around 2000 rather than COBOL, so the skills risk is lower than in banking or tax.

s1.why: Primary sources show that the main register in most in-scope jurisdictions was built before 2005 as an on-prem or mainframe system and is still running. Queensland's ATS went live in 1994 and the 2026 Titles QLD practice manual still describes it. Singapore's INLIS dates from 1998. Malaysia's SPTB was implemented from 1995 and e-Tanah has replaced it in only 10 states. Karnataka's Bhoomi dates from 1999-2001. HMLR's own blog says its register and 140M documents sit on the mainframe. Landgate's CEO said all 37 Torrens jurisdictions ran old systems built around 2000. Caveats: the US county market is split, with Kofile and Tyler hosted systems spreading and AS/400 county systems shown only by anecdote, and no source gives a core build year for Indonesia's KKP.

s2.why: Primary government sources show both very long contracts and multi-year replacements. Victoria signed a 40-year registry concession in 2018 (A$2.86bn) and NSW signed a 35-year concession from 2017. Malaysia announced e-Tanah in 2003 and now targets full Peninsular coverage only by 2030. HMLR's Local Land Charges migration has slipped to end-2028, and it started its transformation in 2018 knowing it would run legacy systems for years. The Philippines LTCP was awarded in 2000 and had not started 5 years later. The concessions cover running the registry, not only software, but they still lock in the platform for decades.

s3.why: There are workarounds, but each source covers only one registry or comes from a vendor. HMLR's Strategy 2025+ says most of its data is paper, scans or PDFs, and that spatial and text data sit in unconnected systems. A UiPath case study (vendor source) says HMLR used 10 RPA bots as a tactical bridge over legacy systems. Kofile, also a vendor source, describes US county staff hand-indexing documents and searching microfiche. Landeed's business is pulling together fragmented state portals in India. No source quantifies spreadsheet use, re-keying or screen-scraping across the main registry systems.

s4.why: No source ties a skills shortage to land registry systems. HMLR does not disclose the language its mainframe uses. The only support is general COBOL statistics (Route Fifty, 2023) and an unverified Erie County, PA AS/400 anecdote whose page did not open. Many registry cores are bespoke Java or .NET systems built around 2000, and those skills are not scarce. Searches for registry-specific skills scarcity found nothing.

reasons_to_stay: The register carries a state guarantee of title (for example, the NSW Torrens Assurance Fund), so integrity outranks speed. HMLR said this explicitly when it delayed LLC to 2028.
Long concession and BOO contracts (35-40 years in AU, BOO in PH) lock in the operator's platform.
Data migration is hard: paper, microfiche and scanned titles (25M in PH, 27M titles at HMLR) must be converted while transactions keep flowing.
Changing the register often needs a statutory amendment (Malaysia amended the National Land Code for SPTB; Queensland's Land Title Act 1994 created ATS).
Procurement is political and slow, with audit-body challenges (e.g. COA questions on the PH LTCP).
Systems are bespoke to local law. Landgate found no off-the-shelf product among about 37 Torrens jurisdictions.

build_vs_buy.criticality_why: Verdict: critical. The call holds. Two tests decide it.
build_vs_buy.best_icp: Sell first to US county recorder and clerk offices serving about 50k-1M people. Five reasons. (1) They buy rather than build. (2) They already pay about $70k-$260k a year. (3) There are about 3,000 counties to sell to. (4) They already buy AI indexing as a separate line item: Fort Bend pays $24.9k a year for aiINDEX. (5) Contracts come up for renewal; Harris County, TX is re-bidding now. The draft's wedge needs two corrections. First, incumbents lock add-ons into their own platforms. Harris Recording Solutions supports and enhances Fort Bend's system only on a sole-source basis through a proprietary integration layer, so a newcomer's add-on may not be able to plug in. Second, larger procurements are competitive. Sedgwick County, KS drew seven bids, from Harris, Catalis, Fidlar, GovOS, Tyler, BIS and Questys. Hillsborough, NH's single bidder was the exception, not the rule. Wagoner County, OK moved to SaaS with its incumbent, Tyler, so it was not an open opportunity. The realistic path: win a full replacement of the recorder system at contract expiry in counties under about 1M people, where a hosted platform with AI indexing and fraud detection built in competes on price against the Tyler, Harris and Fidlar on-prem stack. Leave the national registries and the private concessionaires (Teranet, ISC, the Australian operators) for later. They build their own systems, run multi-year statutory programmes, or are locked into licences lasting 35 to 50 years.

Summary: mid-market firms do not buy this system, so spend is null.

WHY
- Title agencies, conveyancers, lenders and mid-size law firms use registry data. None of them owns a register.
- They pay per use instead. One route is e-recording fees: Simplifile served 2,019 US counties, covering more than 80% of the population, as of December 2019 (ICE press release, verified).
- The other route is search subscriptions. In Fannin County, TX, the county sets Fidlar Laredo end-user prices at $100 a month on the Personal Plan and $250 per subscriber a month on the Business Plan. Fidlar charges the county $20 or $50 per subscriber licence and passes the remainder back as credits (2022 cost sheet, verified).
- In Vermilion County, IL, the reported price is $100-$325 a month. This was not re-checked.

These are usage fees paid to a county or vendor. They are not spend on a land registry system.

smb.evidence:
Summary: SMBs do not buy this system, so spend is null.

WHY
- Small abstractors, solo conveyancers and real estate agents never own or run a register.
- They use registry data through pay-per-search portals. On Fidlar Tapestry, Fidlar pays the county $2.75 per search plus $0.50 per printed image (Fannin contract, verified). The user pays more; the draft's figure of about $8.75 a search was not re-checked.
- The other option is a low-tier Laredo plan, about $1.2k-$3k a year at Fannin's $100-$250 monthly prices.

Note on small counties: small US county recorder offices are SMB-sized by headcount. They are still government buyers, and they are covered in the government segment at about $15k-$60k a year.

name: Loan origination and servicing
systems: ICE (formerly Black Knight) MSP mortgage servicing system: z/OS mainframe, COBOL batch and CICS
ICE Encompass (formerly Ellie Mae) mortgage loan origination system
Finastra Loan IQ (formerly IQ Financial Systems / Misys) commercial and syndicated loan servicing
FIS Commercial Loan Servicing (formerly ACBS) commercial loan system
Sagent LoanServ (formerly Fiserv Lending Solutions) mortgage and consumer loan servicing
Nucleus Software FinnOne / FinnOne Neo retail and SME lending (APAC, India)
Loan modules in core banking systems from FIS, Fiserv, Jack Henry and CSI (US community banks)
In-house servicing systems such as Ocwen's REALServicing
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: The category is more legacy-locked than typical in US mortgage servicing, where one 1960s-era mainframe (MSP) holds 63% of first-lien loans with 5 to 7 year contracts. It is less locked in origination, where Encompass and newer LOS and lending platforms are already cloud-hosted and challengers (nCino, Lentra, Mambu) are winning share.

s1.why: The dominant US servicing core is a pre-2005 mainframe, and primary sources quantify it. Black Knight's FY2022 10-K puts MSP on 32.8M first-lien loans, 63% of the US market. PennyMac's SEC-filed complaint says MSP was 'first developed over 50 years ago' and runs on a mainframe with batch processing. ICE job posts confirm z/OS COBOL/CICS. Other dominant cores also predate 2005: Loan IQ (1990s, about 70% of syndicated loan volume by vendor claim), ACBS (early 1990s) and Encompass (client-server, early 2000s). Caveats: the complaint is a litigant's allegation, and the origination side (Encompass, and FinnOne rebuilt as Neo) is now cloud-hosted. The strength rests on servicing.

s2.why: The 10-K says contracts 'typically span five to seven years', below the 7+ threshold. Deferred conversion costs amortized over 5 to 10 years point to stickiness but do not measure replacement time. The FTC 2023 ICE/Black Knight complaint (para 129) calls LOS switching 'expensive, lengthy, and resource-intensive' but gives no duration. The figure is redacted. The multi-year replacements cited are single-firm cases: PennyMac's MSP replacement ran about 2011 to 2019 (its own complaint), and Newrez's move to Valon only starts in 2027. Lock-in is real, but no primary source quantifies multi-year replacement across the installed base.

s3.why: The evidence is anecdotal or about single firms. The CFPB's 2017 Ocwen suit alleges manual workarounds on an in-house platform (REALServicing), not a dominant vendor system. PennyMac says it built 150+ custom modules around MSP's functional gaps, but those are add-on software, not spreadsheet or re-keying workarounds, and the claim comes from a litigant. The only survey (Kani 2025 via kennek, 56% manual spreadsheet reconciliation) is secondary, UK-only and about reconciliation, not origination or servicing. No primary quantified source shows spreadsheet use, re-keying or screen-scraping on the dominant systems.

s4.why: The evidence is one vendor's job posts plus a generic mainframe statistic. ICE is hiring for MSP and requires 8+ years of z/OS COBOL/CICS, which shows the skill is needed but not that it is scarce. The 71% figure for understaffed mainframe teams (BizTech 2025) is a secondary, cross-industry survey, not specific to this category. Loan IQ, Encompass and FinnOne skills are niche but not shown to be scarce. Encompass administrators are common in US mortgage hiring.

reasons_to_stay: Contracts typically run 5 to 7 years, and conversion costs are amortized over 5 to 10 years (Black Knight FY2022 10-K)
Switching is 'a significant undertaking' with lengthy timelines. ICE itself estimated the first-year cost of switching LOS for a lender (FTC complaint).
Investor and regulator reporting (GSEs, Ginnie Mae, CFPB servicing rules) is already built into incumbent systems. A rebuild risks compliance errors, as the CFPB's Ocwen case shows.
Ecosystem lock-in: ancillary services (PPE, default, data) are integrated with the incumbent LOS or servicing system, and the FTC says assembling them is a barrier to entry
Network effects in syndicated lending: agent banks and the counterparties they serve are all on Loan IQ
Data conversion risk for millions of borrower accounts. Ocwen still had 15% of a ResCap transfer unverified 3 years later.
Big-bank migrations are multi-year programs (PennyMac 2011 to 2019; Newrez to Valon starting in 2027)

name: Custom COBOL and mainframe applications (cross-industry)
systems: IBM Z mainframes running z/OS (MVS lineage) with custom COBOL, PL/I and Assembler applications
IBM CICS Transaction Server (online transaction processing, released 1969)
IBM IMS (hierarchical DB/transaction manager, installed 1968)
IBM Db2 for z/OS and VSAM data files
JCL batch and 3270 'green screen' (TN3270) terminal front ends
Micro Focus (now Rocket Software) COBOL / Enterprise Server
Unisys ClearPath Forward (MCP, from Burroughs 1961; OS 2200)
Fujitsu mainframes (sales end FY2030, support end FY2035)
Broadcom (ex-CA Technologies) mainframe tooling (IDMS, Datacom, Endevor etc.)
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: More legacy-locked than a typical enterprise software category: the dominant stack (z/OS, CICS, IMS, COBOL) dates from the 1960s and holds decades of undocumented business rules, and the vendor still ships new hardware every year, so staying put is cheaper and less risky than migrating.

s1.why: The dominant installed stack is IBM Z running z/OS, CICS (released 1969), IMS (installed 1968) and Enterprise COBOL. Unisys MCP dates from 1961. GAO-25-107795, a primary audit, finds that the 11 most critical US federal legacy systems are 23 to 60 years old. Two Treasury systems among them run on COBOL and Assembly. This sign holds by definition for the category, and IBM's 2022 share-of-top-50-banks figures show the base is still in use.

s2.why: GAO's primary audit is quantified. Of 10 critical federal modernizations flagged in 2019, only 3 were done by Feb 2025. Two of the rest are 5 or more years out, one has no date, and HHS plans run to FY2035. Two of the 11 systems in the 2025 review had no modernization plan at all. The evidence is strongest for government. The private-sector proof is the CBA core replacement (about 5 years, over A$1B), which is one case. It stays strong because the GAO figures span several agencies, but it is close to the line for banks.

s3.why: The only non-vendor evidence is from the Bipartisan Policy Center, a think tank. It interviewed state officials about COBOL unemployment-insurance systems and found paper processes and manual data entry. That covers one government niche, not the dominant bank, insurer and telco base. Screen-scraping of 3270 terminals is real and common, but the evidence comes from RPA vendors (UiPath terminal activities). GAO-25-107795 does not document spreadsheet or re-keying workarounds. No quantified cross-industry source was found.

s4.why: GAO (primary, 2025) says Treasury's COBOL and Assembly systems depend on languages with 'a dwindling number of people available'. It also says agencies pay a premium for specialized staff. Industry surveys add numbers, though most are vendor-commissioned. A 2018 Forrester study found enterprises lost 23% of mainframe staff in 5 years and 63% of those roles stayed unfilled. A Micro Focus survey found 60% of COBOL users name hiring as their top challenge. A 2025 survey found 71% of mainframe teams understaffed. One caveat: scarcity is weaker in IN and PH, where offshore service firms (TCS, Infosys) train mainframe staff at scale.

reasons_to_stay: Proven reliability and throughput: IBM says z17 handles up to 24 trillion operations per second and mainframes process 87% of transactions (IBM Think).
Long, costly, risky rewrites. CBA's core replacement took 5 years and cost over A$1B. GAO warns that undocumented modernization plans raise the odds of cost overruns and project failure.
Business rules are embedded in undocumented code that nobody fully understands.
Gartner (cited by IBM) expects 75% of 'mainframe exit' vendors to pivot or exit by 2030, which makes exit look risky.
Vendors commit to long roadmaps: Unisys ClearPath Forward 2050 and IBM's annual z cycles.
Regulatory and operational risk of migrating core ledgers, payments and tax systems.

build_vs_buy.criticality_why: Verdict: critical. Both tests pass for the commercial buyers who make up most of this market. The differentiation test is weaker for government buyers.
build_vs_buy.best_icp: Sell first to the lower end of enterprise and the upper end of mid-market: regional insurers, regional banks with their own COBOL, and logistics or retail firms running about 400-2,000 MIPS and spending about $1-5M a year on mainframe vendors. Three reasons. They pay the highest price per MIPS (IBM's own TCO deck), so the savings case is strongest. They lack the large in-house teams and long IBM, Kyndryl or Accenture relationships that slow top-50 banks. And they can sign a fixed-price migration quickly, while the largest buyers ($50-150M a year) and national agencies run multi-year procurements dominated by incumbents. A likely fourth reason, that their codebases are small enough to migrate in quarters, is my assumption and not sourced. After landing referenceable wins, move to small and mid-size US state agencies (Wyoming and Kansas scale), then to large banks and federal agencies.

mid_market.evidence:
VERIFICATION SUMMARY. The range of $150K to $3M a year stands. I corrected how one source price was described (Rocket Marketplace); the correction does not move the range.

1. WHO BUILDS IN-HOUSE. Some. Mid-market firms that still run COBOL usually own the application code. They are more likely than enterprises to have done one of three things: (a) outsourced the mainframe to a hosting provider, (b) rehosted the COBOL onto Windows or Linux with Rocket (formerly Micro Focus) Enterprise Server, or (c) moved to a packaged system such as a bank core. Packaged systems are covered by other categories in this study. IBM's 2007 TCO deck describes a 'small mainframe customer' tier averaging 400-600 installed MIPS (verified). That is the realistic ceiling for mid-market buyers.

2. LOW END: rehosted COBOL, about $150-800K a year.
(a) AWS lists Rocket Runtime at $5.55 per CPU core per hour (verified). That is about $48.6K per core per year, so a 4-16 core production estate costs about $0.2-0.8M a year in runtime licence before AWS infrastructure.
(b) AWS's own worked example (dev tools, test and 2 production instances) totals $11,452.16 a month, about $137K a year (verified).

name: Medical billing and revenue cycle
systems: Epic Resolute (Hospital Billing / Professional Billing), built on the Chronicles database and written in M (MUMPS)
Oracle Health (Cerner) Patient Accounting, Soarian Financials and Invision (ex-Siemens/SMS), being folded into RevElate
MEDITECH MAGIC (1982) and Client/Server (1994) financials, migrating to Expanse
TruBridge (ex-CPSI, Healthland) community-hospital EHR and RCM
Altera Digital Health Paragon and Sunrise (ex-Allscripts/Eclipsys)
SAP IS-H patient management and billing (DACH and EU hospitals; mainstream support ends 2027, extended support to 2030)
InterSystems TrakCare (Asia/Oceania, UK, Middle East)
HBCIS patient administration system (Queensland Health, early 1980s) and DXC iPM/webPAS (Australia)
VA VistA (US government, being replaced by Oracle Health)
Indonesia SIMRS (hospital information systems) plus BPJS V-Claim/E-Klaim INA-CBG, often not bridged to each other
Singapore National Billing System (NBS) alongside the Epic-based NGEMR
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Hospital RCM is more locked in than typical enterprise software because billing shares one M-based database with the EHR, so replacing billing means replacing the EHR. But the dominant cores are still actively developed, and most of the manual pain comes from payer connectivity, not the cores' age.

s1.why: The installed base is measured and old. KLAS market share (via HealthSystemCIO, May 2026) puts Epic at 43.7% of US acute hospitals, Oracle Health/Cerner at 21.9% and MEDITECH at 14.7%, about 80% of US hospitals combined. All three cores shipped well before 2005 as on-prem or client-server systems: Epic Resolute in 1987 on Chronicles/M, MEDITECH MAGIC in 1982 and Client/Server in 1994 (Expanse only in 2018), and Cerner Millennium, Soarian and Invision in the 1980s to 2000s. Outside the US the picture is the same: SAP IS-H has run for over 30 years, HBCIS dates from the 1980s, and TrakCare sits on an M database. Caveats: the dates come from Wikipedia and FundingUniverse company histories, not vendor filings. Epic is actively developed and often hosted. Physician-practice billing (athenahealth, eClinicalWorks) is mostly cloud, so this grade applies to hospital RCM.

s2.why: The evidence is a set of public-sector cases, not a category-wide measure. NYC H+H spent $289M over five years on Epic revenue cycle (a Politico reprint). iTnews estimates about seven years to replace Queensland's HBCIS. DSAG says tendering an IS-H successor alone takes about two years. The VA's 10-year Oracle Cerner contract and the LA County and SF 10-year Epic contracts were seen only in search snippets or on blocked pages. No KLAS or survey data on implementation length or typical contract term was found. Replacement also usually means a full EHR replacement, so these timelines describe EHR programs more than billing alone. The sign is plausible and repeated, but anecdotal.

s3.why: The 2024 CAQH Index is a primary, industry-wide, quantified source. Only 35% of medical prior authorizations are fully electronic (X12 278). 39% go through web portals or IVR, which means re-keying, and 22% are fully manual (phone, fax, mail, email). CAQH sizes the remaining savings at about $20B. RCM is also a main market for RPA bots that scrape payer portals. Caveat: the re-keying is driven mostly by payer-side connectivity, not by the age of the provider's billing core. The UC Davis 'dummy appointment' workaround is one anecdote, and the Indonesian SIMRS/E-Klaim re-entry claim comes from a vendor blog.

s4.why: The only cited source is a trade opinion piece (Health IT Outcomes) calling MUMPS programmers a dying breed. It has no labor-market data. Epic skills are scarce mainly because Epic gates certification behind employer sponsorship, not because the skill base is shrinking. Billing analyst roles themselves are configuration work, not M coding. No source quantifies an SAP IS-H/ABAP skills shortage. Surveys do report RCM staffing shortages (for example 63% of providers), but those are about coders and billers, not skills for a legacy system. The sign is plausible but not shown.

reasons_to_stay: Billing is tied into the EHR. Epic Resolute and MEDITECH financials share one database with scheduling and clinical data, so replacing billing usually means replacing the EHR.
Cash-flow risk at go-live. After the UC Davis Epic conversion, staff resorted to 'dummy' appointments to keep certain billing running.
Very high cost and long timelines: $289M over five years for NYC H+H revenue cycle, about 7 years and $200M+ for Queensland's PAS replacement.
Payer and regulatory rules are encoded over decades (US payer edits, German DRG billing in IS-H, BPJS INA-CBG, PhilHealth case rates). Rebuilding them is risky.
Vendors keep extending support. SAP IS-H has extended maintenance to 2030 and a transition option to 2033. Queensland bought extended HBCIS support to 2023.
Procurement friction. DSAG estimates two years just to tender an IS-H successor, and public buyers must run formal tenders.
Incumbent consolidation keeps customers in place. Oracle is folding Soarian and Invision into RevElate, IKS Health bought TruBridge, and MEDITECH reports 84% legacy retention.

TEST 1: Does the business stop or lose its licence if billing fails? It nearly stops, but the licence is safe. Billing is how a provider gets paid, and an outage cuts off cash within days. Evidence: the Change Healthcare cyberattack (Feb 2024). An AHA survey of nearly 1,000 hospitals (9-12 March 2024) found 94% had a financial impact and 82-83% had cash flow affected (the PDF says 82%, the web page 83%). Nearly 60% of the hospitals affected put th
build_vs_buy.best_icp: Sell first to mid-market multi-site and specialty physician groups and MSOs (about 20-300 providers). They spend about $200K-$4M a year on billing. They buy rather than build. They can change billing vendors without replacing a hospital EHR (though often with their practice management system). They decide faster than hospitals, which run board reviews and multi-year tenders. Enterprise and government budgets are 10-30x larger, but their billing sits inside Epic or Oracle, so an entrant there can sell only an add-on layer (the route AKASA and Adonis take), not a replacement.

enterprise.evidence: WHO: large health systems and academic medical centres, with about $2B or more in net patient revenue (usually 10+ hospitals). BUILD OR BUY: they buy. Checked and kept as rare. Almost none write their own billing system. They run the billing module of their EHR (Epic Resolute or Oracle Health Patient Accounting), because billing shares one database with scheduling and clinical records. LA County's June 2026 memo (checked) requires one integrated database across EHR, population health and revenue cycle, and says only Epic now meets that. Epic has 43.7% of US acute hospitals and 56.9% of beds (KLAS via HealthSystemCIO, checked). Enterprises do keep the work around the software in-house: revenue cycle departments, analytics and automation bots. R1's 10-K lists 'internal RCM departments of healthcare organizations' as a competitor (checked). So 'build' here means doing the operations in-house, not writing the system. SPEND ANCHORS (licence, maintenance, hosting, clearinghouse and vendor services; staff excluded). (1) Steady state. LA County DHS was quoted a 10-year total cost of ownership above $200M for Oracle's revenue cycle module alone, so more than $20M a year (memo checked). (2) Implementation year. NYC Health + Hospitals (2017): $289M over five years for Epic revenue cycle across 11 hospitals and 70+ clinics, about $58M a year (checked). CORRECTION: the article says the software was already bought in the earlier $764M Epic deal, and the $289M pays for staffing to customise

mid_market.evidence: WHO: two groups. (a) Community hospitals of about 25-200 beds, which run MEDITECH (14.7% of US acute hospitals, checked), TruBridge or Altera Paragon. (b) Multi-site and specialty physician groups and MSOs with about 20-300 providers, which run athenahealth, NextGen, eClinicalWorks or AdvancedMD. BUILD OR BUY: they buy. Checked and kept as rare. Neither group can afford to build a billing system. Many outsource the billing work. Weston County Hospital (Wyoming) authorised talks with Inova RCM to take over billing, coding and credentialing (checked; no cost given). government.evidence: WHO: publicly owned hospital systems. In the US: county and city systems (NYC H+H, LA County DHS, Alameda Health System, Harris, Parkland, Jackson) and the VA. Abroad: public hospital authorities such as Queensland Health, Singapore's public clusters and DACH public hospitals on SAP IS-H. BUILD OR BUY: some build, more often than in other segments. Kept as 'some', with one example corrected. Real in-house builds: the VA built VistA (including its billing module) and is now replacing it with Oracle Health. Singapore runs a separate national billing system next to its Epic-based NGEMR. Many Indonesian public hospitals develop or adapt their own SIMRS hospital systems (earlier research, not re-checked). CORRECTION: Queensland's HBCIS is an old system kept running on extended support, not an in-house build. iTnews (checked) says it is nearly 30 years old, runs in all of the state's public hospitals, and fell out of vendor support in 2015. It shows public buyers delaying replacement, not building their own. US county systems buy, through formal tenders or sole-source deals. SPEND ANCHORS. (1) LA County DHS memo, June 2026 (checked): Oracle's revenue cycle module was quoted at more than $200M over 10 years, more than $20M a year. The county is now opening sole-source talks with Epic for EHR, population health and revenue cycle. (2) NYC H+H: $289M over five years, about $58M a year, but as noted under enterprise this was implementation staffing and training, not recurring software.

name: Mortgage servicing
systems: ICE (formerly Black Knight) MSP Mortgage Servicing Platform: z/OS mainframe, COBOL batch + CICS, DB2/VSAM, vendor-hosted
Sagent LoanServ (ex-Fiserv MortgageServ), now marketed as the Dara cloud platform
FICS Mortgage Servicer (on-prem / hosted, for mid-size banks, credit unions and commercial servicers)
Phoebus Software platform (UK/Ireland mortgage and savings administration, designed 1989)
Target Group (Tech Mahindra) loan management / servicing platform (UK)
Nucleus Software FinnOne / FinnOne Neo lending suite (India, SE Asia)
Core-banking loan modules (Temenos, Finacle, Silverlake and similar) used for mortgage servicing at Asian banks. Inferred, no source found for this study.
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Mortgage servicing is more legacy-locked than a typical enterprise software category because one vendor-hosted COBOL/CICS mainframe system (ICE MSP) runs roughly half or more of US mortgage loans, and network effects across subservicers, MSR transfers and GSE reporting make leaving costly. That lock-in is mostly a US phenomenon: elsewhere servicing sits inside general core-banking or lending suites.

s1.why: The dominant US system is ICE (formerly Black Knight) MSP. Black Knight's FY2022 10-K, a primary and quantified source, puts it at about 36M active loans against a US market of about 66M first and second liens and lines of credit. ICE's own 2026 MSP job post asks for z/OS COBOL batch, CICS, JCL and DB2/VSAM, which confirms the mainframe stack independently of PennyMac's partisan '50-year-old mainframe' claim. The 10-K itself only calls MSP 'a SaaS solution' and does not describe the technology. Outside the US the evidence is weak: Phoebus (UK, 1989) has no share data, and no specific pre-2005 servicing core was tied to the SE Asian regions. The strong grade rests on US dominance only.

s2.why: The evidence does not meet the 7+ year or multi-year bar for the dominant system. The FY2019 10-K figure is '12 to 18 months, or longer' to switch, which is not multi-year, and the FY2022 10-K only says 'long-term contracts' with no length. Published MSP renewals are 5 years (Cenlar, EverBank). The one 7-year term found is Mr. Cooper's commitment to Sagent, a single deal reported in trade press. A 7-year LoanCare renewal on MSP appeared in search results but was not verified. PennyMac's multi-year, module-by-module exit is one partisan case. The lock-in is real (30-year client tenures such as Cenlar), but neither duration test is shown directly.

s3.why: The evidence is indirect, and the main source is a litigant. PennyMac says it built 'hundreds' of bolt-on modules around MSP and that data is downloaded from and uploaded back to MSP. CFPB Supervisory Highlights Issue 11 (2016) found IT staff manually overriding data fields during servicing transfers, which is a transfer-specific finding. No primary or quantified source shows spreadsheets, re-keying or screen-scraping as routine practice across MSP or other servicing users.

s4.why: The only evidence specific to this category is one ICE job post for the MSP team. It asks for 8+ years of z/OS COBOL/CICS and treats AI coding tools as a plus, which suggests scarcity but does not quantify it. The Deloitte survey cited by BizTech (71% of firms say mainframe teams are understaffed) covers financial services in general, not mortgage servicing. No mortgage-specific vacancy, wage or retirement data was found.

reasons_to_stay: Switching takes 12 to 18 months or longer, and the cost is significant (Black Knight FY2019 10-K).
Regulators expect extensive testing and validation before a servicer changes major systems (PennyMac complaint).
Servicing transfers carry CFPB exposure: lost loss-mitigation documents and late payment crediting during data moves.
Investor, GSE and agency reporting (Fannie, Freddie, Ginnie, FHA/VA) is already built and certified on the incumbent.
Multi-year contracts (for example Mr. Cooper's 7-year commitment to Sagent) and long renewals lock buyers in.
Network effects: subservicers, MSR buyers and vendors integrate to MSP formats, so leaving it adds friction on every transfer.
Vendor litigation risk: Black Knight sued PennyMac in 2019 when it left MSP.

build_vs_buy.criticality_why: VERDICT: critical. The call holds, with two factual fixes noted below. WHY IT IS CRITICAL. (1) The business stops if it fails. The servicing system is the book of record for every loan. It posts payments, runs escrow for tax and insurance, drives collections and loss mitigation, and sends remittances and reports to investors and to Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac and Ginnie Mae. If it goes down, cash stops reconciling, the servicer misses CFPB Regulation X timelines and investor servicing-guide deadlines, and its agency approvals and state licences come under threat. (2) It is where the firm competes.
build_vs_buy.best_icp: Sell first to US mid-market servicers with 25K to 500K loans that are about to choose a platform anyway (independent mortgage banks moving servicing in-house from a subservicer, large credit unions and regional banks outgrowing FICS or a core-banking module, and state housing finance agencies at renewal), because they spend about $0.5M to $10M a year, rarely build, and leaving a subservicer is a cleaner cutover than a top-10 MSP deconversion, which takes 12 to 18 months and can draw a PennyMac-style licence claim, while SMB budgets of $25K to $300K are too small to fund agency-grade compliance; note that Valon took the other route, proving its platform on its own 810K-loan book before selling that book to Carrington.

enterprise.evidence: WHO: the largest US banks, nonbank servicers and subservicers, each with roughly 500K to 4M+ loans. UWM (in-house servicing on ICE MSP from 2025) sits at the low end of this tier given its retained book, so it belongs here rather than in mid-market. BUY OR BUILD: most buy, a meaningful minority build. Buying: ICE MSP runs about 36M active loans (Black Knight FY2022 10-K; this count includes first and second liens) and, per ICE's MSP product page, 7 of the top 10 servicers in the J.D. Power 2024 study. Sagent reports 16M+ active loans and 40+ clients, with Mr. Cooper (3M+ loans) as a top customer. Building: PennyMac built its own SSE platform and left MSP from 2019, and the arbitrator confirmed PennyMac owns SSE outright. Mr. Cooper built a servicing platform, then sold it to Sagent in March 2022 for $260M total consideration (a 19.9% Sagent stake plus $9.9M cash) and committed to license it back for 7 years. Valon built ValonOS and ran its own 810K-loan book on it before Carrington bought the servicing business. Three top-tier builders out of a few dozen enterprise servicers is 'some', not 'rare'. (Removed: the claim that Lloyds and JPMorgan service mortgages on Thought Machine. No source supported it, and JPMorgan's Thought Machine use is for UK retail deposits. Also removed: 'tiered per-active-loan pricing' for the Mr. Cooper licence, which the cited filings do not state.) HOW MUCH, three ways. (1) Average unit price: Black Knight servicing software revenue was $838.9M in 2

mid_market.evidence: WHO: regional banks, independent mortgage banks newly bringing servicing in-house, large credit unions and nonprofit lenders, each with roughly 25K to 500K loans. BUY OR BUILD: they license a vendor platform and almost never build. A custom build means recreating escrow, investor accounting and Reg X logic, which only top-tier scale has justified (PennyMac, Mr. Cooper, Valon). Public examples of buying: Ruoff Mortgage, Union Home Mortgage, Pulte Mortgage, Fahe and Mortgage Clearing Corp chose MSP, Evergreen Home Loans chose Sagent's Dara platform (2026), and FICS sells to mid-size banks and credit unions. The usual alternative to buying software is outsourcing the whole job to a subservicer (Cenlar, Dovenmuehle, LoanCare). That is a services spend, not a software spend. (Moved: UWM was listed here, but its book puts it at the enterprise tier.) HOW MUCH: apply the roughly $20 to $25 per loan a year implied by Black Knight's servicing revenue divided by active loans. 25K loans gives about $0.5M to $0.6M, 50K loans about $1M to $1.25M, and 400K loans about $8M to $10M. Smaller books often pay a higher effective rate because of contract minimums. RANGE: about $0.5M to $10M a year. CORRECTION: the low end was $1M, but the tier starts at 25K loans and the stated unit price gives $0.5M there, so the low end is lowered to match its own math. Confidence: low to medium. This is derived from the unit price; no mid-market contract value was found in public sources.

smb.evidence: WHO: community banks and credit unions holding about 1K to 25K mortgages. The pool is large: 4,238 FDIC-insured institutions (FDIC, Q2 2026) and 4,214 federally insured credit unions, of which only 748 have assets over $500M (NCUA, Q2 2026; both verified). Many qualify for the CFPB small-servicer exemption (5,000 loans or fewer, all self-originated or owned). BUY OR BUILD: they almost never build. They do one of three things: (a) sell loans servicing-released or hire a subservicer, (b) use the loan module of their core banking system, or (c) license a low-cost in-house package such as FICS Mortgage Servicer. FICS's site promises a low initial investment and a nominal monthly support and maintenance fee, but publishes no prices. Fully loaded cost to service a performing loan averaged $176 in 2024 (MBA), and software is only a slice of that. HOW MUCH: no public price exists. The estimate applies $15 to $25 per loan a year for software plus hosting to books of 2K to 15K loans, which gives about $25K to $300K a year. Institutions using a core-banking module may pay little or nothing extra, so the true floor is lower. RANGE: about $25K to $300K a year. Confidence: low. There is no contract or pricing page with numbers, and nothing found contradicts the estimate by more than 2x.

government.evidence: WHO: US state housing finance agencies that service their own loans, and federal direct lenders. BUY OR BUILD: both buy. Pennsylvania HFA (about 63K loans, $4.9B) moved from LSAMS, which it had used for in-house servicing since 1999, to Black Knight MSP in Q2 2019 (National Mortgage News). Virginia Housing renewed MSP after 25 years. USDA Rural Development licenses LoanServ (Fiserv, now Sagent) for its Single Family Housing Direct portfolio. Many smaller HFAs avoid owning a system by using a subservicer. HOW MUCH, from public contracts (all verified in the USAspending API): USDA's annual LoanServ support, upgrade and licence task orders were $3.47M (FY2015, Fiserv), $3.0M (April 2021 to March 2022, Sagent, which includes licences), $2.2M (FY2024, Sagent), plus a 2025 to 2030 order with $4.6M obligated so far. The FY13 and FY14 figures ($2.27M, $2.34M) were not rechecked. So one federal agency pays about $2M to $3.5M a year for servicing software alone. Adding its separate UniFi origination-system orders, USDA's total Sagent spend runs about $4M to $5M a year. For an HFA with 20K to 100K loans, the $20 to $25 per-loan rate implies about $0.5M to $2.5M a year. No HFA contract value was found. RANGE: about $0.5M to $5M a year. Confidence: medium at the federal end (real contract data), low for HFAs (derived). Outside the US, state housing lenders such as Thailand's Government Housing Bank are buyers, but no contract values were found.

name: Payroll and HR administration
systems: SAP ERP HCM / SAP HR & Payroll (R/3, ECC 6.0), with country payroll versions
Oracle PeopleSoft HCM (HRMS)
Oracle E-Business Suite HRMS / Payroll (e.g. NHS ESR)
Infor Lawson S3 HR/Payroll (ex-Lawson Software)
UKG (Kronos) Workforce Central time and attendance, on-prem
ADP legacy in-country and global payroll platforms (ADP iHCM, ADP Global Payroll), being moved to ADP Lyric / Workforce Now
In-house COBOL mainframe government payroll (e.g. California Uniform State Payroll System, Colorado CPPS)
IBM AS/400 (IBM i) payroll applications at municipalities and mid-market firms
Spreadsheet-based payroll (Excel) at SMBs
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: Payroll is more locked-in than typical enterprise software at the deep end: statutory tax, award and union rules are hard-coded, errors are not tolerated, and the evidence shows multi-year, billion-dollar public-sector replacements. It is less locked-in at the top and the bottom, where Workday (65%+ of the Fortune 500) and SaaS bureaus such as ADP RUN and Gusto already hold much of the installed base.

s1.why: First-ship dates are solid. SAP R/3 HR shipped in 1992, PeopleSoft HRMS in 1989, Lawson started as mainframe software, and California's payroll is a mainframe set of 12 systems, some nearly 50 years old. SAP's cloud Employee Central Payroll still runs the old SAP HCM payroll engine. But no source puts a number on the installed-base share of these cores. The one quantified share figure points the other way: Workday's 10-K says it serves 65%+ of the Fortune 500 on a core first shipped after 2005. US SMB payroll is mostly SaaS or bureau (ADP RUN, Gusto). So pre-2005 cores dominate public sector, higher education and part of mid-to-large enterprise, but not the category as a whole.

s2.why: Two separate primary, quantified cases on different stacks. (1) California LAO: the CSPS replacement costs about $1.2bn, takes about 6 years and completes Sept 2031. It follows the 21st Century/MyCalPAYS attempt, which began in 2004 and was suspended in 2013 after nearly a decade. (2) NHS England and Wales: the Oracle EBS-based ESR, which pays 1.9m staff, moves to a 15-year, GBP 1.4bn (inc. VAT) Infosys contract, and ESR support runs to 2035. SAP HCM extended maintenance to 2030 and H4S4 to 2040 extend the timeline further. Caveat: the quantified evidence is all public sector. Private-enterprise replacements are usually 12-36 months.

s3.why: The primary evidence is one 2013 municipal audit (Killeen TX): paper timecards are re-keyed into an AS400 and every check is recalculated in Excel. The better quantified source is the EY-PayrollOrg Payroll Pulse Survey (2022-23): 40% use SQL-fed spreadsheets and 18% manual processes as their primary way of working with payroll data. That covers data and reporting work, not core processing, and the survey does not tie it to legacy cores. Cloud payroll users report the same habit. The 51% spreadsheet figure is a vendor-cited poll (Strada/Alight).

s4.why: The only primary evidence is California LAO Report 3590 (2017), where the State Controller reports trouble hiring mainframe staff for the payroll system covering about 260k employees. The 2025 LAO CSPS report does not repeat this. InfoWorld (2008) is secondary. Nothing shows scarce SAP HCM, PeopleSoft or Lawson skills, which make up most of the installed base, or any skills gap in APAC or India. SAP HCM consultants are still abundant, and the market is moving toward SuccessFactors ECP.

reasons_to_stay: Payroll is mission-critical and has zero tolerance for error. Queensland Health's 2010 SAP payroll go-live underpaid or failed to pay about 78,000 staff and cost about AUD 1.2bn, which makes buyers very risk-averse.
Deep local statutory logic (tax, social security, awards and union agreements, e.g. PPh 21/BPJS in Indonesia, Australian awards) is embedded and tested in the old system.
Vendors keep extending support (SAP HCM to 2030 and H4S4 to 2040; PeopleSoft rolling to at least 2036), which removes any forcing deadline.
Replacement is a reimplementation, not an upgrade (e.g. Kronos WFC to UKG Pro WFM), and needs parallel payroll runs and data migration.
Public-sector procurement cycles and long managed-service contracts (NHS ESR: 15 years) lock incumbents in.
Integration with GL, time and attendance, pensions and benefits, and banks.

reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: More locked-in than a typical enterprise category. Decades of member benefit history and statutory rules must be migrated exactly, and many dominant buyers are single government funds, so replacement takes 5 to 15 years. Australia's super market is the exception: post-2010 platforms and frequent fund mergers make it less locked-in.

s1.why: FIS Omni/Relius is the dominant US DC recordkeeping engine (650 clients, 68m participants). The vendor's own retirement lead says it was built in COBOL more than 30 years ago and is only being rebuilt for cloud in 2026. Public plans show the same pattern in their own releases: Washington DRS was replacing a 30-year-old system in 2023, Massachusetts SRB a 38-year-old one in 2010, NY MEBEL ran on z/OS, and CalSTRS used its legacy system until 2025. Caveats: Australia's leading core (Bravura Sonata, launched 2010) is after 2005, and the UK's Altair has no disclosed first-ship date. So this is strong for the US and public sector, and less certain for AU and UK.

s2.why: Several primary agency sources each quantify a long replacement. CalSTRS's Pension Solution started pre-implementation in 2010, got budget approval in 2014 and went live in September 2025, with a $523m budget plus $105m post-go-live. Washington DRS signed a 4-year implementation plus 2 years of support with Sagitec (2023). EPFO's CITES 2.01 was approved in 2021 and went live in July 2026. FIS's own Omni rebuild took 4 years. Capita seeks 5 to 10 year TPA terms. Multi-year replacement is the norm across the dominant buyers.

s3.why: The direct evidence is vendor-authored. Sagitec's TRS case study describes re-keying across systems and employers sending data on paper or disk, and Aware Super's 'paper-based legacy systems' quote is also vendor-adjacent. UK industry material (TPR record-keeping research and PASA, both reported second-hand) says about a third of schemes keep non-digital records and that data gathering and calculations are manual. That points to paper and archive records, not quantified spreadsheet or screen-scraping workarounds on top of the dominant platforms. Plausible, but not primary or quantified.

s4.why: The main citation is a single 2013 Computerworld article about one system (NY MEBEL). The audit behind it came from NY DFS and the Comptroller disputed it. COBOL, CICS, DB2 and OmniScript skills for FIS OmniPlus appear in job and CV listings, but no source quantifies a shortage. Nothing was found for UK, AU or Asian provident funds. Dated and anecdotal.

reasons_to_stay: Benefit rules span decades of legislative changes and member history (DB accrual, tranches, transitional protections) that must be migrated exactly. HESTA moved more than a decade of data and still had a members-locked-out cutover period
Regulatory and fiduciary risk: payment errors to retirees are highly visible, and boards prefer incumbent stability
Long outsourcing and TPA contracts (Capita seeks 5 to 10 years) bundle software and administration
Challenger financial fragility: GROW Inc carried going-concern audit doubts and needed client debt and equity support before MUFG agreed to acquire it in 2026
Big-bang regulatory deadlines (Dutch Wtp by 2028, UK pensions dashboards) push funds to extend incumbents rather than switch mid-reform
Concentrated incumbent ecosystems (Heywood Altair across LGPS, FIS Omni across US recordkeepers) supply frameworks, interfaces and skilled staff
Fund mergers (AU consolidation from 1,656 to 771 APRA funds in 5 years) often settle on the acquirer's existing platform instead of a new one

name: Port and container terminal operating systems (TOS)
systems: Navis SPARCS / SPARCS Express (Kaleris), on-prem predecessor of N4
Navis N4 (Kaleris), first site live 2006
PSA CITOS (in-house, 1988)
Hutchison Ports nGen (in-house, 2003)
Tideworks Mainsail / Mainsail Vanguard (SSA Marine subsidiary)
Total Soft Bank CATOS (Korea)
RBS TOPS / TOPX (Australia)
Pelindo legacy TOS / PTOS-M being consolidated onto ILCS TOS Nusantara (Indonesia)
Operator in-house legacy TOS (for example Patrick Terminals' 30-year in-house system replaced by N4 in 2020; seen only in search snippets)
reason: strong evidence on at least 1 sign and strong + half weak >= 2.5
differentiator: This category is more legacy-locked than typical enterprise software. A TOS is real-time control of cranes, gates and automated equipment, so cutovers need operational shutdowns and cores run 20 to 30 years. It is less locked than mainframe categories, because the dominant product (Navis N4, 2006) is a vendor-supported Java platform that gets regular upgrades and is moving to cloud.

s1.why: The market's dominant lineages began as on-prem client-server systems before or around 2005. PSA CITOS dates from 1988 and Navis SPARCS from 1989 (academic history). Hutchison nGen went live in 2003, RBS TOPX shipped in 1996, and Tideworks Mainsail launched in 1999. Primary customer sources confirm long-lived pre-2005 cores in production. GPA ran SPARCS/Express at Garden City from fall 2000 until its N4 cutover in April 2022. Patrick's CIO described replacing a '30-year-old legacy TOS' with N4 in 2020. Two caveats. The market leader, Navis N4 (389 terminals in GPA's FAQ, 500+ Navis ports per Kaleris), first went live in 2006, so it is a mid-2000s Java client-server rewrite rather than mainframe or midrange. No source documents mainframe or midrange architecture anywhere in this category.

s2.why: Primary operator sources show decades of tenure and multi-year replacement programmes at the largest operators. GPA ran SPARCS/Express for about 21 years (2000 to 2022). Patrick ran an in-house TOS for about 30 years. APM Terminals set a target to standardise its global portfolio on N4 by end-2021, but Aarhus only went live in March 2022, after data-migration problems that raised truck turn times. DP World Australia's consolidation of 19 systems onto N4 ran over several years. Single-site projects take 12 to 24 months, but that figure comes only from a vendor (INTECH). Contract lengths of 7+ years are not directly documented. The evidence is tenure and programme duration.

s3.why: The best quantified evidence is a global Tideworks survey with no stated sample size or year. In it, 89% of terminals use a TOS, yet 56% still rely on email and spreadsheets, only 33% use APIs, and 45%+ report integration problems with partners. That is vendor marketing, and it describes manual coordination around the TOS with partners, not re-keying or screen-scraping of the TOS itself. Portwise, a consultancy blog, says small terminals plan berths on spreadsheets or whiteboards. No independent or primary source quantifies workarounds at the large N4, CITOS or nGen sites.

s4.why: All of the scarcity evidence comes from one recruiter, KiTalent, across content-marketing pieces on Rijeka, Genoa and Sohar. They claim 8 to 11 months to hire senior N4 specialists, an N4 vacancy left open for about 11 months, and roughly 200 to 250 Navis/Kalmar automation engineers in the whole GCC. These pieces are unverified and possibly templated. The scarcity they describe is vendor-specific configuration know-how for a current product (N4, Java/Groovy), not a dying language or platform. No APAC, US or independent labour-market data was found.

reasons_to_stay: A TOS is mission-critical real-time control. Failed cutovers hurt operations badly: Felixstowe's June 2018 switch from Navis to Hutchison nGen caused lost boxes and truck queues of up to 16 hours (seen in search snippets; the Seatrade article returned 403).
Cutovers need a full operational shutdown window (GPA stopped operations overnight for N4) and 12 to 24 months of implementation.

Deep integration with automated equipment, gates, RFID, EDI and port community systems (PD Ports' Navis role lists SPARCS, MCP, Fast gate, WhereNet RFID, Camco Autogate, VBS). Every interface has to be re-done.
Data migration of 10+ years of container, vessel and customer history takes 4 to 8 months.
Big operators treat their in-house TOS as a competitive asset (PSA CITOS, Hutchison nGen) and build the next generation in-house rather than buy.
There is a small, concentrated vendor field, and specialist TOS staff are hard to hire. Both raise switching risk.

WHO BUYS. Global and regional multi-terminal operators running about 10 to 60 terminals each: PSA, Hutchison, DP World, APM Terminals, COSCO Shipping Ports, TIL/MSC, ICTSI, SSA/Carrix.

BUILD OR BUY: building is common. The operators split into two camps.
- Builders: Hutchison (nGen, US$10M budget 2001-2005, verified), DP World (CARGOES TOS+, 70+ sites, verified), PSA (CITOS, 1988, not opened). SSA/Carrix owned the vendor Tideworks from its founding in 1999 until Diversis Capital bought a majority stake, announced 1 Oct 2026 (verified). Tideworks serves 130+ facilities.
- Buyers who standardise on one vendor: COSCO Shipping Ports signed a global Navis N4 subscription in March 2018 (verified). COSCO then ran 38 ports, but the article does not say N4 went live at all 38. APM Terminals calls N4 the 'world standard' across its network (verified).
